text: The fix reproduces the defect it fixes. MEASURED: delete the Commit() from B's OnRun and B still emits info, same finding, count unchanged. B's golden line is byte-indistinguishable from 'there is no escalation witness in this span at all' -- exactly why ws-d50-pos is worthless as a guard today. The control C does not catch it either: with C's OnRun Commit() deleted, C stays medium because its helper carries the escalation alone. And A is not a differential for B: they differ in FOUR ways at once (committer position, committer form, manager identity, manager branch).
evidence: Design v2 makes A and B ONE-TOKEN TWINS: identical chain, identical bodies, the only delta being `local procedure RunAll()` versus `trigger OnRun()`. opus measured that pair directly: A = medium, B = info. A cap break then flips B to medium and a span/commit-machinery break flips A to info, so neither can rot silently behind the other. Plus opus's belt, taken: a gap test asserting B's OnRun id IS in the seed span's routines_in_span AND is the SeedKind::ExplicitCommit commit_routine_id -- pinning the precondition directly instead of inferring it from a severity value that also means 'nothing happened'. ROUND 2 (opus, MEASURED): the twins alone do NOT close it — with B's Commit() removed line-count-preservingly, B's finding is BYTE-IDENTICAL (same id, same fingerprint, still info, same line). Only the gap test closes K1, and calling it a 'belt' licenses dropping it. So the gap test is now REQUIRED, not optional: it is the only assertion that distinguishes 'capped' from 'nothing happened'. The twins stay, because they are what makes the OTHER direction (a span/commit break flipping A from medium to info) observable.

text: The C control has a one-edit vacuity mode that yields ZERO findings rather than a wrong severity. backward_cone visits a committing caller but never expands it, so if C is written as a CHAIN (OnRun commits -> Helper commits -> seed) the walk stops at Helper, the OnRun never enters the span, there is no transaction-managing routine, and the seed is skipped silently. Measured: a chain fixture produces count 0. The r4 anti-degenerate check is >= 1 per FIXTURE, so A alone would satisfy it while B or C vanish unnoticed.
evidence: Design v2 states the constraint the table left implicit: C's two committers must be INDEPENDENT callers of the seed, never a chain. And the matrix now pins findingCount EXPLICITLY at 3 rather than relying on the per-fixture >= 1 anti-degenerate check, which cannot see a case disappearing. ROUND 2 (opus, MEASURED): my wording WAS the vacuity mode — 'independent callers of the SEED' measures count=0. Corrected: C's two committers must be independent callers of a shared TRANSACTION-MANAGING routine that calls the seed (or the seed must itself be transaction-managing).

text: The issue's second ask -- 'once the fixture exists, revisit whether onrun-codeunit belongs in the list' -- needs to say what evidence would settle it, not merely promise to revisit.
evidence: A6 states the decision procedure: with the twins in place, removing onrun-codeunit from the list flips B medium<->info observably, so the question becomes 'is an OnRun's Commit() provably at the top of its own transaction?'. d50's own doc already answers no (Codeunit.Run can be called from arbitrary code and AL has no nested transactions, so the callee joins the caller's open transaction). The kind therefore STAYS, and the fixture is what makes that answer falsifiable rather than asserted. ROUND 2 (fable): the stated reason argued the OnRun's Commit() is MORE consequential, which is the opposite of what cap 2 tests. The conclusion (onrun-codeunit STAYS) is right for the public-procedure reason: cap 2 asks whether the committer is provably at the top of its own transaction, and an entry point reachable from arbitrary callers is not — the same reason public-procedure is listed. Reworded on that ground.
